text: Given the root of a binary tree, return its nodes' values in postorder.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — postorder means: at every node, the whole left subtree comes out first, then the whole right subtree, and the node itself comes last. Is that right?

Then here's the property I want on the table early, because it's the reason postorder exists at all. In postorder, a node never comes out before its children — both subtrees are fully emitted first, so the root is always the very last value. That's why postorder is the order you free a tree in, and the order for any bottom-up value like height, subtree sum, or subtree size. The children's answers are always ready before the parent needs them.
Can the tree be empty? And are there any constraints on the input size?
Empty is allowed, return an empty list. Up to one hundred nodes, any shape.

Let me run through the example. Root one has children two and three. Two has children four and five, and five has children six and seven. Three has only a right child, eight, and eight has a left child, nine. Left side first: under two we get four, then five's children six and seven, then five, then two. Right side: nine, then eight, then three. Finally the root, one. So four, six, seven, five, two, nine, eight, three, one.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to run a preorder and then reverse it. That's a very common belief, and it's wrong — I'll show the counterexample in review. This problem reminds me of a plain depth-first search, with the emit moved to the end. Postorder is what DFS does on the way back up, so I write the recursion and push after both calls return.

Here's the plan. One: if the node is empty, return. Two: recurse into the left child, then the right child. Three: push the node's value last. I'm using one shared vector passed by reference, and each call appends only at the end, so its block stays in one piece. One thing worth flagging — postorder is not the reverse of preorder. Preorder is node, left, right; reversing it gives right, left, node, but postorder is left, right, node. The correct identity: postorder equals the reverse of the node, right, left walk. There's a trade-off here: that identity gives a short iterative solution with one stack, but it needs a reverse pass and a second explanation, and the plain recursion reads exactly like the definition. I'll go recursive. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The main function just calls the helper and returns the vector. The helper stops on null, recurses left, recurses right, and only then pushes the value. One thing worth flagging — the push sits after both calls, so every value is written on the way back up the stack. That's what makes this the right skeleton for any bottom-up computation: by the time that last line runs, both children are done. Two details I'd keep as-is: the base case is the empty link, not a leaf check, which would crash on an empty tree and drop every leaf. And the ampersand on the vector is required, or each call fills a copy and a non-empty tree returns empty.

Let's dry-run the code on the same tree, expected four, six, seven, five, two, nine, eight, three, one. The row that matters is the last one: the root is pushed at step nine, after all eight other nodes. Every row works that way: a node goes out only after everything under it. That matches. Corner cases: an empty tree returns empty at once. A single node makes two empty calls, then pushes one. And one, two, three breaks the reverse-of-preorder idea: reversed preorder is three, two, one, but true postorder is two, three, one. That false rule only holds on chains, where no node has two children.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is linear: exactly two n plus one calls, one per node plus one per empty link, since an n-node binary tree has exactly n plus one empty links. Constant work per call. Space is O of h for the call stack, where h is the height; the output vector is linear, but that's the answer itself. In the worst case the tree is a chain, so h equals n; a balanced tree is about log n. At a hundred nodes neither is a problem. Oh, one more thing — this version only reads the tree. But if I reused this skeleton to delete the tree, postorder is the safe order: in preorder I'd free a node and then read its child pointers, which is a use-after-free.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You led with the real guarantee — a node is emitted only after everything below it — and tied it to freeing a tree and to bottom-up values, instead of just reciting left, right, node. You called out the postorder-is-reverse-of-preorder belief as false and gave the smallest counterexample, plus the correct identity with node, right, left. And you explained why that false rule survives testing: it only holds on chains, where no node has two children. Good work.
